newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean acres seen rising in 1997 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean acres seen rising in 1997 - analysts.

text.p: The soybean market's current high prices, very low U.S. soybean stocks, and the "Freedom to Farm" agriculture law are all seen contributing to an increase in U.S. soybean acreage in 1997, oilseed analysts said.
Analysts estimated plantings at 64 to 66 million acres, with most estimates near 65 million. U.S. farmers planted 64.2 million acres to soybeans last year.
"I think that farmers have heard from everyone that the prospects for oilseeds are much brighter than are those for feedgrains," said analyst Joel Karlin at Everen Securities.
At its annual outlook conference on Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast 1997 soybean plantings at 65.3 million acres.

Analysts pointed to the current new crop corn/soybean price ratios as favoring soybeans. The market's high soybean prices will "buy" U.S. acreage as farmers consider which crop will deliver the largest return, they said.

CBOT November soybeans were trading at $7.05 on Wednesday and December corn at $2.79. A year ago, soybeans were trading at $7.33 but corn at $3.80, with worries about low world stocks of feedgrains pushing corn as high as $5.54 by July.

"I think because (soybean) stocks are so low right now we're trying to get to an area where we're buying some acres, or at least rationing demand," said Don Roose, grain analyst with U.S. Commodities in West Des Moines, Iowa.
The USDA projects soybean stocks at 140 million bushels on September 1, 1997, against 183 million a year earlier.
Analysts also said price comparisons between cotton and soybeans could also boost soybean acreage in the Southeast.
"Beans are favorably positioned in price," said Travis Miller, extension agronomist at Texas A&M University in College Station.
"Those people that are teetering on the edge may take a look at beans," Miller said.
Last year's heavy insect infestation in cotton and the resulting poor yields might mean some cotton growers, tired of the problems, are ready to switch crops, Miller said.
USDA this week forecast 1997 cotton plantings at 14 million acres, down 4.6 percent from 1996. USDA said the loss in acreage was due to more favorable corn and soybean prices.
A year ago NYCE cotton was trading at $1.00 to $1.15 a lb, while December cotton Wednesday was quoted at 77.40 cents.
Wayne Hoener, soybean product manager for Asgrow Seed Co in Kalamazoo, Michigan, also expects to see soybeans and corn replace cotton acreage in the South.
"A lot of it is going to have to do with price, but also 'Freedom to Farm' and the weather," Hoener said.
Under the new U.S. Farm Bill, farmers are free to base planting decisions on market factors rather than complex formulas of "base acres" or past plantings.
"I think it (the law) favors soybeans more so than corn, because you always had to at least plant your base (corn acreage)," Karlin said. "But that's not the case any more."
Analysts also see the new farm law increasing use of "one-to-one" crop rotation plans, where soybean and corn crops will be rotated annually.
Other areas where soybean acreage expansion is seen is on acres that had intially been intended for winter wheat and on some spring wheat acres in the Northern Plains, analysts and agronmists said.
In the eastern Midwest soft red winter wheat belt from Ohio to Missouri, soybeans are often double-cropped on the SRW acres that are harvested beginning in June.
